sources.news_title: McConnell returns home after two-month medical absence
sources.text:
US Senator Mitch McConnell said he was returning home on Thursday after nearly two months in hospital and rehabilitation, as the 84-year-old's extended absence strains a tight Republican majority.
The former Republican Senate leader was hospitalised in mid-June, but speculation about his condition swirled for weeks as his office provided no further details.
The veteran lawmaker from Kentucky finally broke his silence on July 12, saying he had been treated for a fall and loss of consciousness, and had since been moved to a rehab facility.
He also revealed that he had developed a minor case of pneumonia while in hospital.
In a statement Thursday, McConnell said he had finally been "discharged from the rehabilitation centre to continue my recovery at home."
"On the advice of my doctors, I'll maintain an intensive regimen of physical therapy from home during the state work period," he said, referring to the Senate's August recess.
He apparently will miss key votes this week before the recess, including on the confirmation of US President Donald Trump's pick for US attorney general.
Several Republican senators have expressed concerns about Trump's nominee Todd Blanche -- who is the president's former personal lawyer – raising the possibility that the vote will be delayed.
McConnell did not say if he would make his Senate return when the chamber reconvenes in September.
He is not seeking reelection and is due to retire in January. (AFP)
Edited by Cecil Wong

Mitch McConnell Discharged From Hospital After Nearly Two Months, Continuing Recovery at Home
Sen. Mitch McConnell has been discharged after nearly two months of hospitalization and rehabilitation following a June health scare, but the 84-year-old Kentucky Republican is not yet returning to the Senate.
McConnell announced Thursday that he is returning to his Washington, DC, home, where he will continue an intensive physical therapy program. He did not provide a specific date for when he expects to return to Capitol Hill.
The senator was rushed to the hospital on June 14 after being found unconscious at his residence. Emergency dispatch communications initially referenced a possible cardiac event, fueling questions about the severity of his condition as McConnell remained hospitalized for weeks.
McConnell later revealed that doctors determined he had not suffered a heart attack or stroke. He also said he had no broken bones, concussion, tumors or hemorrhages, though he acknowledged that he briefly lost consciousness and subsequently developed a mild case of pneumonia while receiving treatment.
After leaving the hospital, McConnell spent additional time at a rehabilitation facility before being cleared to continue his recovery at home. He thanked doctors, nurses, therapists and hospital staff for their care while also expressing appreciation for the support he and his wife, former Transportation Secretary Elaine Chao, received during the ordeal.
McConnell said he plans to remain engaged in Senate business while undergoing physical therapy during the chamber’s state work period. He has remained in contact with his staff and Republican colleagues throughout his absence and has participated in some committee business through proxy voting.
His lengthy absence sparked widespread speculation online about his condition, including false rumors that he was “brain dead.” Senate Majority Leader John Thune and other Republican senators pushed back against those claims after speaking directly with McConnell while he was hospitalized.
The episode adds to a series of health concerns McConnell has faced in recent years. In 2023, he suffered a concussion and fractured rib after falling at a Washington event and later experienced two widely publicized incidents in which he appeared to freeze while speaking publicly.
McConnell has not announced exactly when he will resume voting in person. For now, the longtime Kentucky senator will continue recovering at home while staying involved with his staff and Senate colleagues, marking a significant step forward after nearly two months away from Capitol Hill.

sources.text:
(WASHINGTON) — Republican Sen. Mitch McConnell, after weeks of in-patient care following a fall in mid-June, announced via a statement from his office on Thursday that he has been discharged from a rehabilitation center and will continue his recovery at home.
“Earlier today, I was discharged from the rehabilitation center to continue my recovery at home,” McConnell said in a statement. “Elaine and I are grateful for the many well wishes and support from friends, colleagues, and Kentuckians, and for the attentive care I’ve received from excellent doctors, nurses, therapists, and hospital staff.”
“On the advice of my doctors, I’ll maintain an intensive regimen of physical therapy from home during the state work period, and I’ll continue to engage with my staff and colleagues on important Senate business,” McConnell added.
McConnell was first hospitalized on June 14 for reasons that were initially undisclosed by his office.
While his office has released two photographs of McConnell since his hospitalization, the Kentucky senator has not been seen in public.
Late last month, Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear called on McConnell to either “verbally” show proof to Kentuckians that he can still serve in the Senate or to resign from Congress.
In a statement issued on July 12, nearly a month later, McConnell said he was hospitalized due to a fall that left him briefly unconscious. He also said he had to deal with a “mild case of pneumonia.”
In that same July 12 statement, McConnell said he had been moved from the hospital to a rehabilitation facility to recover.
The former Republican leader has not been seen on Capitol Hill since June 11.
McConnell has said he intends to finish his term, which expires in January. The seven-term senator has already said he does not intend to seek reelection in January.
The Senate is expected to recess until mid-September in the coming days. McConnell’s statement suggests he won’t be seen in the Capitol until at least then.
Before departing for recess, the Senate is expected to take up acting Attorney General Todd Blanche’s nomination to permanently lead the Department of Justice. With McConnell’s absence, Blanche can only afford to lose two Republican votes.

McConnell says he’s left rehab center to ‘continue my recovery at home’
Kentucky Republican doesn’t indicate when he will return to the Capitol
Sen. Mitch McConnell’s office said Thursday he was released from a rehabilitation center and is continuing his recovery at home.
“On the advice of my doctors, I’ll maintain an intensive regimen of physical therapy from home during the state work period, and I’ll continue to engage with my staff and colleagues on important Senate business,” a statement from the former majority leader says.
The Kentucky Republican, 84, was hospitalized June 14 after a fall and subsequent pneumonia, and has missed weeks of votes in the Senate. That included a markup earlier Thursday in the Agriculture Committee, where he “voted by proxy.” But proxy voting doesn’t count toward advancing a bill to the full chamber floor, causing the farm bill the committee was working on to stall.
His statement did not note when he would return to work in the Senate, which is scheduled to return in mid-September after its August work period.
McConnell’s extended absence has raised concerns, including from Kentucky’s Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear, who on Monday worked to dispel online rumors Aug. 3 was the last day for him to call a special election if the seat became vacant.
“I know there are a lot of folks wondering about the significance of August 3 regarding a potential Senate vacancy. I want everyone to know that this date has no legal impact on my options should there be a vacancy this year,” Beshear posted to X. “Worth a reminder, right now, there’s one less vote for the SAVE Act, Trump’s war with Iran, or the potential replacement of a SCOTUS justice.”
Senate Majority Leader John Thune told Gray News it had been “several weeks” since he and his predecessor had last spoken.
“There are, in this day and age, a lot of conspiracy theories and of course, with doctoring and AI and all that, there’s all kinds of stuff that gets done on social media,” Thune said when asked if people deserve more evidence McConnell is of sound body and mind. “I think, at the end of the day, those are issues that are between him and the people of Kentucky, the people he serves and represents.”

U.S. Senator Mitch McConnell has been released from a rehabilitation center, 53 days after his June 14 fall, marking his first significant step back toward normal Senate engagement. His return home signals that the Senate’s longest‑serving GOP leader is resuming work—albeit remotely—during a critical stretch of the August state work period.

He noted that, on doctors’ advice, he will keep up “an intensive regimen of physical therapy” and remain actively engaged with his team and colleagues on key Senate matters.
McConnell's fall in June led to hospitalization and extended rehabilitation, sidelining him from public appearances and raising questions about how long he would remain off the Senate floor.
His release suggests a gradual return to routine duties, though his physical recovery continues to shape the pace and visibility of his work.
News of McConnell's return home was met with optimism on Capitol Hill on Thursday, with senators from both parties wishing him well, despite many telling Newsweek they had not yet spoken with him and were hearing of the development for the first time.
What Happened to Mitch McConnell?
McConnell’s fall left him briefly unconscious and triggered a battery of medical tests as doctors worked to determine the cause. He later revealed that he did not suffer broken bones, a concussion, a stroke or a heart attack, but he did develop a mild case of pneumonia while hospitalized.
The incident revived long-standing concerns about his mobility, which he has said stems from childhood polio.

The Senator says he intends to engage with his colleagues and his staff but leaves out the most important people of all—the people of Kentucky.”
When Was Mitch McConnell Hospitalized?
McConnell was hospitalized on June 14 after the fall at home. His office initially said only that he was receiving “excellent care,” but weeks passed without meaningful updates, intensifying public and political pressure.
By mid‑July, he confirmed that he had undergone extensive testing to rule out serious conditions and had transitioned from hospital care to a rehabilitation center.
Who is Mitch McConnell’s Wife, Elaine Chao?
Chao, McConnell’s wife, is a former U.S. Secretary of Transportation and Secretary of Labor, and a longtime figure in Republican administrations. She has been a visible presence throughout his recovery, appearing in the photo McConnell released from the hospital and referenced in his statement thanking supporters.
Chao’s public support has also served as a counterweight to online speculation about McConnell’s condition, with the couple presenting a united front amid rumors and misinformation. Her involvement emphasizes the personal dimension of McConnell’s recovery and the role she plays in managing public perception and private care.
How Many Votes Has McConnell Missed?
McConnell has missed 47 roll‑call votes since his absence began in mid‑June—100 percent of votes during that period. In total, he has missed 56 votes in 2026, roughly 27 percent of all Senate votes this year.
His absence has drawn scrutiny from political observers and constituents, though his office continues to operate normally, handling constituent services and legislative coordination. The missed votes highlight the practical impact of his recovery on Senate operations, especially during a year of tight margins and high‑stakes legislative battles.
Is Mitch McConnell Returning to the Senate?
McConnell has not been medically cleared to return to the Capitol in person. According to updates from the Office of the Attending Physician, daily evaluations continue, but no date has been set for his physical return.
For now, he will work remotely from Kentucky, participating in Senate business during the state work period. His gradual recovery suggests a phased return, though the pace will depend on medical guidance and his ability to resume full duties.

He also pointed to historical precedent showing that senators have returned under extraordinary circumstances only when a single vote could determine the outcome.
“Sick senators have gone to remarkable lengths when one vote was indispensable,” Burgat said, citing John McCain’s dramatic 2017 vote on Obamacare repeal, Pete Wilson’s ambulance arrival for a budget vote in 1985, and California Senator Clair Engle pointing to his eye to vote “aye” on the 1964 Civil Rights Act cloture motion.

Topline
Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., said Thursday he’s been discharged from the rehabilitation center where he was recovering from a June fall, issuing a statement hours before the Senate is set to break for a five-week recess.
Key Facts
McConnell said he will “maintain an intensive regimen of physical therapy from home during the state work period” and “continue to engage with my staff and colleagues on important Senate business.”
McConnell has given two statements on his health since he was hospitalized following a June 14 fall that left him briefly unconscious, prompting calls for more transparency about the 84-year-old senator’s condition.
In his initial statement on June 13, accompanied by a photo of him sitting upright in a hospital bed alongside his wife, former Transportation Secretary Elaine Chao, McConnell said he was still in the hospital after the fall and a “mild case of pneumonia,” but said he didn’t suffer any broken bones, concussion, heart attack, stroke or have any “tumors or hemorrhages.”
In a second statement on July 28, with a similar photo of him and Chao, he said he’d been moved to a rehab facility but wasn’t yet medically cleared to leave and wouldn’t attend a weekend political picnic in Kentucky; he also missed the funeral of his longtime Senate colleague, Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C.
His doctor said in the statement last month that his “bout with childhood polio continues to be a significant factor in his mobility.”
McConnell’s absence has complicated the Senate’s busy legislative calendar, as Republicans have a slim 53-47 majority in the upper chamber, and without McConnell, business on the Senate appropriations committee has come to a halt as the committee is split 14-14, meaning legislation can’t advance without bipartisan support.
Read Statement On McConnell’s Discharge In Full
“Earlier today, I was discharged from the rehabilitation center to continue my recovery at home. Elaine and I are grateful for the many well wishes and support from friends, colleagues, and Kentuckians, and for the attentive care I’ve received from excellent doctors, nurses, therapists, and hospital staff.
“On the advice of my doctors, I’ll maintain an intensive regimen of physical therapy from home during the state work period, and I’ll continue to engage with my staff and colleagues on important Senate business.”
Tangent
Kentucky’s Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear has repeatedly urged McConnell to call into a news program or issue a video statement to prove he is capable of continuing to serve. Beshear must call a special election to fill McConnell’s seat if it becomes vacant, but there is some uncertainty surrounding the timeline since the November general election to fill McConnell’s seat is less than three months away. Some Kentucky lawmakers have speculated that the deadline for calling a special election in the event of a vacancy was Aug. 3, given the deadlines for notifying local officials of the special election. Beshear, however, suggested the date “has no legal impact on my options should there be a vacancy this year,” he wrote Monday on X, adding, “Worth a reminder, right now, there’s one less vote for the SAVE Act, Trump’s war with Iran, or the potential replacement of a SCOTUS justice” with McConnell absent.
Key Background
McConnell is set to retire at the end of the year after 42 years in the Senate. He has experienced a series of health issues over the years and has been seen using a wheelchair or the assistance of aides to move around the Capitol recently. In 2023, he froze while speaking in front of reporters twice in a span of less than two months. His office attributed the episodes to lightheadedness, but physicians who viewed the footage said his symptoms mirrored those of mini seizures. He also experienced two serious falls in 2023 and 2024.

Sen. Mitch McConnell’s (R-KY) continued absence from the Senate is no longer just a health story.
It’s turning into a real threat to President Trump’s agenda with Republicans now governing on a margin so thin that a single missing vote could sink one of Trump’s key nominations and derail a key piece of Trump-championed legislation.
A deadline some believed could force a decision on McConnell’s Senate seat came and went this week without resolution, and the GOP is feeling the heat.
SUCCESSION WATCH: Mitch McConnell's Senate absence stretches into its third month as an Aug. 3 deadline that could have triggered a special election came and went with no resolution.
Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear says the date carries no legal weight — but pointedly reminded… pic.twitter.com/RSS8v7HmNM
— Fox News Politics (@foxnewspolitics) August 5, 2026
McConnell has been out of the public eye since early June and is already set to retire when his term ends this year.
Speculation had built around August 3rd as a key date in forcing McConnell’s return, with some assuming Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear (D) would be forced to call a special election that day if McConnell’s seat were vacant.
Beshear moved to shut down confusion over the Aug. 3 deadline directly. “I know there are a lot of folks wondering about the significance of August 3 regarding a potential Senate vacancy,” he wrote on social media.
“I want everyone to know that this date has no legal impact on my options should there be a vacancy this year.”
That didn’t happen. But the deadline’s non-event status did little to ease the bigger question hanging over the GOP: how much longer can they afford to be short a vote on the votes that matter most to Trump?
According to insiders, every day McConnell stays out is a day Republicans have one less vote for the SAVE Act, for Trump’s actions on Iran, and for a potential Supreme Court replacement, all items Beshear himself was quick to point out in recent reports.
The next most immediate domino in McConnell’s absence could be President Trump’s pick to lead the Department of Justice, acting Attorney General Todd Blanche, whose confirmation could now come down to a single vote.
However, Kentucky’s succession law changed significantly in recent years, and unlike most states, the governor no longer has the power to simply appoint a replacement.
That process was tested earlier this year following the sudden death of Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-SC).
If McConnell’s seat opens up, Beshear would be legally required to call a special election rather than hand-pick a successor — meaning any vacancy could leave Trump’s agenda without a full Senate vote for months, not just weeks.
In response, McConnell’s office pointed back to his most recent public statement, issued July 27, in which he said doctors still had not cleared him to return.
“I’m still working hard to get back to my full schedule of work in the Senate and in Kentucky, keeping up with intense physical therapy per my doctors’ orders,” McConnell said at the time.

sources.text:
U.S. Sen. Mitch McConnell has been discharged from the rehabilitation center where he had been recovering since his June fall and will continue his recovery at home, according to a statement released by his office Thursday.
The news comes 10 days after McConnell’s office last provided an update on his condition, when he had not yet been medically cleared to leave the rehabilitation facility.
“Earlier today, I was discharged from the rehabilitation center to continue my recovery at home,” the Aug. 6 statement from McConnell’s office says. “Elaine and I are grateful for the many well wishes and support from friends, colleagues, and Kentuckians, and for the attentive care I’ve received from excellent doctors, nurses, therapists, and hospital staff.”
The statement continues: “On the advice of my doctors, I’ll maintain an intensive regimen of physical therapy from home during the state work period, and I’ll continue to engage with my staff and colleagues on important Senate business.”
A new photo of McConnell was not provided by his office for the Aug. 6 update.
The Kentucky Republican has been recovering since a June fall at his Washington-area home that led to a four-week hospitalization followed by inpatient rehabilitation. His office has said the lingering effects of childhood polio have been a significant factor in his recovery and mobility.
